claims.text: A conventional impurity-controlled low-alloy ferritic steel will exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition under systematic tempering.
At intermediate tempering temperatures, impurity elements such as phosphorus segregate to grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary impurity segregation induces temper embrittlement in low-alloy ferritic steel.
Temper embrittlement is not observed in compositionally complex or high-entropy alloys.
The initial low-alloy ferritic steel has a homogeneous microstructure.
Tempering at 300°C, 400°C, 500°C, and 600°C can span the regions below, within, and above the narrow temper-embrittlement window.
High-entropy alloys do not exhibit temper embrittlement under the proposed heat treatments.
Segregation of embrittling impurities such as phosphorus to grain boundaries triggers the transition in mechanical behavior.
At lower tempering temperatures, the steel microstructure retains ductility.
At intermediate tempering temperatures, grain-boundary impurity segregation reduces ductility and produces brittle behavior.
At higher tempering temperatures, impurities re-dissolve or diffuse away from grain boundaries.
Removal of impurities from grain boundaries at higher tempering temperatures restores ductility.
The low-alloy steel will have high ductility after low-temperature tempering, a significant ductility drop in a narrow intermediate range, and recovered ductility after high-temperature tempering.
High-entropy or compositionally complex alloys will not exhibit the dramatic ductile–brittle–ductile transition predicted for the low-alloy steel.
Temper embrittlement is absent in high-entropy alloys subjected to similar heat treatments.
The proposed behavior occurs only in conventional alloys with controlled impurity levels.
Alloys with high compositional complexity are immune to the proposed transition.
The transition temperatures and magnitude of ductility loss and recovery depend on impurity levels and microstructural factors.
